Harley-Davidson El Sicario Is the Bad Boy of the Chicano Kin
46 photos
Photo: Thunderbike
In all the ways that matter, the term sicario doesn't really mean anything good. Which kind of raises the question why someone would choose it to describe a Chicano-style custom motorcycle based on the Harley-Davidson Heritage.
The crew responsible for the build and giving it this name is German-based Thunderbike . That would be a group of people with such a passion for the American-made motorcycles that they've literally created hundreds of builds based on them.
With such a large portfolio under their name, the Thunderbike people have pretty much gone through all the possible custom styles. Chicanos, naturally, are properly represented.
We've covered quite a lot of these builds here on autoevolution, but I have to say, so far I haven't seen anything as extreme as El Sicario. Maybe it's the color scheme chosen for it, or the flamboyant bodywork it wears, or maybe something else, but that's the way it makes me feel.
It's unclear what model year the Heritage it is based on was born into, but that matters little in the grand scheme of things. What matters is the fact that the bike is so heavily modified that it instantly captures the attention.
It wears wheels much larger than they originally were, sized 23 inches at the front and 18 inches at the rear – the proper dimensions for a build of this kind. The huge wheel at the front also displays a massive, 340 mm brake disc, accompanied by fresh calipers.
Above each wheel, Thunderbike fitted massive fenders, sculpted in such a way as to visually stretch the two-wheeler and make it pop out. Up on the frame, a special seat made of cowhide and crocodile skin can be seen.
The way the bike feels to the rider has changed a lot compared to the base motorcycle . At the front, the fork, now packing an air ride system, comes with an extra six degrees of rake, achieved by fitting a dedicated triple tree, and a 14-inch (35 cm) handlebar fitted on old-school risers is what allows control.
At the rear, it too supported by an air-ride suspension, there is a custom swingarm kit, and the brake disc, usually fitted on the right side, has been moved to the left, which is also where the license plate has been moved.
Other minor touches do wonders in modifying the look of El Sicario, including the custom headlight fairing, the lights, the mirrors, and the several covers that dress the design in key places.
Thunderbike left the bike's stock Softail frame and its Milwaukee-Eight engine in their factory configuration, but even those might seem modified when drowned in so many custom modifications.
When everything was said and done, Thunderbike went for a bright green color for the body, adorned with special pinstriping. The effect is, as you can see, simply mesmerizing.
The German crew spent around $16,000 on the parts that went into the build alone, and that shows. Sadly, we have no info on how much was spent on the paint job and the man-hours invested in this.
